query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Nanoscale precipitation of Hf-rich phases in refractory high-entropy alloys can improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance.

generation.conditions: High-temperature (up to 1000 °C) and mechanical loading conditions
generation.predicted_outcome: Improved high-temperature mechanical properties (strength and ductility) with minimal impact on room-temperature performance and density
generation.baseline: Refractory high-entropy alloys without Hf-rich phase precipitation
generation.boundary: Temperature range: up to 1000 °C, loading conditions: mechanical loading
generation.uncertainty: Optimal Hf content and precipitation morphology for maximizing high-temperature mechanical properties while minimizing density and preserving room-temperature performance

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare refractory high-entropy alloy samples with varying Hf content (0, 0.03, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 at%) and characterize their microstructure and mechanical properties at room temperature and high temperatures (up to 1000 °C) using tensile testing and microscopy
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the addition of Hf does not lead to significant improvements in high-temperature mechanical properties (strength and ductility) while preserving room-temperature performance and limiting density, the hypothesis is falsified.

Dual-phase high-entropy alloys with excellent room temperature and high-temperature properties have been widely studied as potential high-temperature structural materials. However, interface weakening causes its high-temperature performance to decline at higher temperatures, severely limiting further development. In this study, a series of Al17Cr10Fe36Ni36Mo1Hfx (x = 0, 0.03, 0.15, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.8 at%) alloys were prepared to study the effect of Hf content on the microstructure and mechanical properties of the matrix alloy. The results indicate that with the addition of the Hf, the Hf-rich phase began to precipitate at the interface and inside the B2 phase in the matrix alloy. In contrast, the morphology of both the FCC and B2 phases had no noticeable change. With the increase in Hf content, the high-temperature strength and ductility of the alloy first increased and then decreased, while the room temperature performance remained almost unchanged. As we all know, the alloying of metals with certain specific elements can very effectively improve alloy properties through various strengthening methods such as precipitation strengthening, solution strengthening, and interface strengthening [,,,]. Hf is an essential alloying element for both the interface strengthening of superalloys and the strengthening of the Ni-Al B2 phase [,,,,,]. Recently, some studies have shown that adding a small amount of Hf to a single-phase FCC high-entropy alloy could improve the room-temperature mechanical property of the alloy without significantly reducing the ductility of the alloy through the precipitation of intermetallic compounds such as Ni7Hf2 and Laves phases [,]. However, these studies mainly focus on single-phase high-entropy alloys, and the addition of Hf is relatively large, usually more than one atom. Therefore, the effect of trace Hf addition on the properties of the alloy at room temperature and high temperature is worthy of in-depth investigation.

Moreover, after annealing at 1000 °C for 10 h, the W10 RHEA slightly demonstrated increased hardness and strength compared with the as-prepared specimens. As shown in Table 3, the hardness increased from 639 ± 23 HV to 647 ± 13 HV, while the strength increased from 1867 ± 52.5 MPa to 1930 ± 45 MPa. This indicates that the (TiVCrZr)100−xWx RHEAs may have better mechanical properties at high temperature. As shown in Figure 7a, the microstructure of the annealed specimens still exhibited four different contrasts including white, bright, gray and dark regions, which is similar to the microstructure of as-prepared specimens (Figure 7b). Thus, the (TiVCrZr)100−xWx RHEAs may possess higher thermostability and have potential for high temperature applications.
